841.event_title: Paulo Freire's forty-hour literacy programme at Angicos
841.place: Angicos, Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil
841.event: In 1963 the educator Paulo Freire led a government-funded pilot programme in the small town of Angicos in north-eastern Brazil, in which nearly 300 poor rural workers and adolescents were taught to read and write in about forty hours of instruction. Teachers built lessons around words and images drawn from the learners' own lives, aiming at political awareness as well as literacy. The pilot was meant to lead to a national literacy programme, but that plan was halted after the military coup of 1964 and Freire left Brazil.
841.explanation: Angicos became the founding example of Freire's view that illiteracy, more than lack of money, kept the poor powerless, and his methods were later used in literacy campaigns around the world.
841.tie_back: The kural says the lack of understanding is the real poverty, and Freire's programme treated the workers' want of literacy, rather than their want of wealth, as the deprivation to be overcome first.
841._accuracy_note: Reasonable illustration of knowledge as the deeper wealth, but the programme addressed literacy rather than the folly of the unwise that the chapter mainly targets.

842.event_title: The Boston Red Sox sell Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees
842.place: Boston and New York, United States
842.event: In late December 1919 Boston Red Sox owner Harry Frazee, who was short of money, agreed to sell the contract of his star player Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees owners Jacob Ruppert and Tillinghast Huston. The Yankees paid 25,000 dollars in cash and three promissory notes, about 100,000 dollars in all, and the sale was announced in January 1920. Ruth went on to his greatest years with the Yankees.
842.explanation: The sale is remembered as one of the most lopsided deals in sports history, transforming the Yankees and stripping Boston of its best player.
842.tie_back: The kural says ironically that when a fool gives something away gladly, the cause lies in the good fortune of the receiver, and the Yankees owed their great prize to Frazee's willingness to part with it rather than to any skill of their own.
842._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it was a sale for needed cash rather than a glad gift, and Frazee's folly is a popular judgement rather than a documented fact.

843.event_title: Muhammad ibn Tughluq's token currency ends in mass forgery
843.event: Between about 1329 and 1332 Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq of Delhi attempted a fiduciary currency, issuing brass and copper tokens that were meant to pass at the value of silver tankas. The tokens were forged on a massive scale, and the experiment became a total failure. The sultan then redeemed all the tokens, forged and genuine alike, in gold and silver at the treasury's expense.
843.explanation: The scheme, imposed without safeguards against forgery, inflicted on the sultan's own treasury a loss that no rival had managed to cause and became a byword for ill-judged policy.
843.tie_back: The kural says the suffering fools bring on themselves exceeds anything their enemies could inflict, and the sultan's ill-planned currency drained his own treasury more effectively than any foe.
843._accuracy_note: Strong fit for self-inflicted harm, though historians note the experiment was a genuine policy attempt rather than simple foolishness.

844.event_title: General Braddock spurns Native allies and is defeated at the Monongahela
844.place: Monongahela River, near present-day Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States
844.event: In 1755 General Edward Braddock led a British army trained in European parade-ground drill against the French at Fort Duquesne. He had very few Native American guides, a shortage sources link to his own treatment of the Native leaders he met, and he appears to have ignored intelligence on the French position offered through a Mohawk ally. On 9 July 1755 his advance column was attacked near the Monongahela River by a smaller French and Native force, more than half his men were killed or wounded, and Braddock was mortally wounded.
844.explanation: The defeat kept the Ohio Valley in French hands for three more years and made Braddock a lasting example of a commander undone by confidence in his own methods.
844.tie_back: The kural defines folly as the arrogance that says we are the wise ones, and Braddock's reliance on his own European ways over local knowledge led his army into disaster.
844._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit; sources describe the accusation of arrogance as common rather than proven, so the event field keeps to documented actions.

845.event_title: Henry Ford's ignorance of history is exposed at his libel trial
845.event: Henry Ford sued the Chicago Tribune for libel after it called him an ignorant idealist and an anarchist. At the 1919 trial in Mount Clemens, the newspaper's lawyers questioned him on subjects outside his expertise, and he mangled basic facts of American history, placing the American Revolution in 1812 and describing Benedict Arnold as a writer. The jury found in Ford's favour but awarded him only six cents in damages.
845.explanation: The trial made the world's most famous industrialist an object of ridicule on subjects he had pronounced on publicly, even as his genius in manufacturing remained undisputed.
845.tie_back: The kural warns that pretending to know what one never learned makes people doubt even what one has mastered, and Ford's public pronouncements beyond his field brought scorn that touched his whole reputation.
845._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the damage done by venturing beyond one's learning, though the sources do not show his manufacturing reputation actually suffered.

846.event_title: Richard Whitney, former head of the Stock Exchange, is exposed as an embezzler
846.event: Richard Whitney, president of the New York Stock Exchange from 1930 to 1935 and a model of Wall Street respectability, secretly took money entrusted to him, including funds from the Exchange's Gratuity Fund for members' families, the New York Yacht Club, of which he was treasurer, and bonds from his father-in-law's estate. In March 1938 the Exchange discovered that his firm was insolvent and Manhattan District Attorney Thomas E. Dewey charged him with embezzlement. Whitney pleaded guilty and was sentenced to five to ten years in Sing Sing prison.
846.explanation: The fall of the man who had stood for the Exchange's integrity captivated a nation still struggling through the Great Depression.
846.tie_back: The kural calls it folly to cover the body carefully while leaving one's faults uncorrected, and Whitney's immaculate public respectability concealed wrongs that he never put right.
846._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it illustrates outward respectability masking uncorrected faults, but the kural's image of clothing is only loosely matched.

847.event_title: Russian armies send uncoded radio orders before Tannenberg
847.event: In August 1914 two Russian armies invaded East Prussia but transmitted many of their orders over open radio without encoding them. German forces intercepted the messages, learning the location and direction of march of the Russian Second Army and that the First Army was not coming to its aid. Using this knowledge, the German Eighth Army encircled and almost destroyed the Russian Second Army at the Battle of Tannenberg at the end of August.
847.explanation: Tannenberg became a classic lesson in the cost of failing to guard vital information, as the Russians handed their enemy the secret that decided the battle.
847.tie_back: The kural says the fool who lets a precious secret slip does great harm to himself, and the Russian commands broadcast their own plans to the enemy who then defeated them.
847._accuracy_note: Strong fit for the traditional reading about failing to guard a vital secret, though the cause was confusion over codes rather than one person's folly.

848.event_title: Challenger is launched despite engineers' warnings
848.place: Kennedy Space Center, Florida, United States
848.event: On the evening of 27 January 1986, engineers at the booster manufacturer Morton Thiokol, including Roger Boisjoly, argued that the space shuttle Challenger should not be launched in the forecast cold because the rubber O-ring seals in the booster joints might fail. After a teleconference with NASA, Thiokol managers reversed the engineers' no-launch recommendation. Challenger broke apart shortly after lift-off the next morning, killing all seven crew members, and the Rogers Commission found that O-ring failure in the cold had caused the accident and that flawed decision-making was a contributing cause.
848.explanation: The disaster became a standard case study in engineering ethics, showing how an organisation can refuse a clear warning from those who know the facts.
848.tie_back: The kural condemns the one who will not do right even when told and cannot see it for himself, and the managers who overrode the engineers neither heeded the warning nor recognised the danger on their own.
848._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for refusing advice, though the failure was institutional rather than one person's lifelong folly as the kural describes.

849.event_title: Geologists dismiss Alfred Wegener's continental drift
849.event: On 6 January 1912 the German scientist Alfred Wegener presented his theory that the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart to a geological meeting in Frankfurt, and he expanded it in later books. Most geologists of his day reacted with hostility, attacked Wegener personally as an outsider, and dismissed the idea as a fairy tale. Only decades later, in the 1960s, did new evidence lead to the theory of plate tectonics and the acceptance of his central idea.
849.explanation: Wegener's case shows how a person who presents an unwelcome truth can be treated as the foolish one by those who are sure of their own view.
849.tie_back: The kural says whoever tries to show the truth to those who will not see ends up looking like the fool, because they are certain they already see everything their own way, and Wegener was ridiculed by geologists who were the ones in error.
849._accuracy_note: Strong fit; the geologists were learned specialists rather than fools in the ordinary sense, and his theory did lack a convincing mechanism at the time.

850.event_title: Alfred Russel Wallace wins the flat-earth wager on the Bedford Level
850.place: Old Bedford River, the Fens, England
850.event: In January 1870 John Hampden, who maintained that the Earth was flat, offered a wager of up to 500 pounds to anyone who could prove its curvature. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace accepted, and in March 1870, using markers along a six-mile straight stretch of the Old Bedford River, showed the curvature to the satisfaction of the referee, John Henry Walsh, editor of The Field. Hampden refused to accept the verdict and pursued Wallace with abusive letters and attacks for years afterwards, and was widely regarded as a crank.
850.explanation: The episode is remembered as a case of a man who flatly denied an established fact even after it was demonstrated before an agreed referee.
850.tie_back: The kural says whoever flatly denies what the wise of the world affirm will be regarded as a demon and kept apart, and Hampden's denial of the Earth's curvature after it had been shown to him left him a byword for obstinate folly.
850._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the denial is a clear match, but Hampden's being shunned is a matter of reputation rather than a documented act of exclusion.
